extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles for forming and evaluating names, definitions, propositions, and syllogistic reasoning (precision of terms, connotation vs denotation, real vs verbal propositions, treatment of existence and imaginary subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of connotative names — avoid vague/polysemous terms
rubrics_metrics.description: “Take the familiar term Stone. ... Such a term is wholly unfit for accurate reasoning, unless hedged round on every occasion by other phrases; as building stone, precious stone, gall-stone, etc.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not employ broadly applied, polysemous names in rigorous reasoning without explicit qualification. If a common name covers heterogeneous cases with no uniformly present attribute, either restrict its application or qualify it each time (examples: building stone, precious stone, gall-stone). Recognize that methods of definition fail when community of application is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a precise technical meaning for 'to connote' when analysing concrete general names
rubrics_metrics.description: Author insists on using 'to connote' to express how a concrete general name marks the attributes involved in its signification; this technical use differs from James Mill's broader sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing how names relate to attributes, use a narrowly defined term ('to connote') to distinguish this specific mode of implying attributes from more general verbs like 'involve' or 'imply'. This ensures clear communication about what is tacitly referred to by a name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotation determined by predicate-ability (test of what a name denotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The test of what a name denotes is what it can be predicated of.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish what a name denotes, check which things you can truthfully predicate that name of. Use predication as the operational test of denotation (e.g., if you can predicate 'not-white' of a sound or smell, then it denotes those things). This helps resolve disputes about scope of negative and other names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predication implies a percipient mind (subjectivity of attributes)
rubrics_metrics.description: “To ascribe any attribute to an object, necessarily implies a mind to perceive it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that attributing properties presupposes a perceiving subject; discussions of attributes should acknowledge the role of the percipient. This affects how one frames questions about qualities 'in the thing itself' versus qualities as perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories are analyses of predicates (generalizations of predication), not merely classifications of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories 'seem to have been rather intended as a generalization of predicates; an analysis of the final import of predication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing categorical schemes, focus on the kinds of predicates that can be made about things (their final import) rather than attempting an exhaustive enumeration of 'namable things'. Ask 'Under what categories can we predicate regarding X?' rather than 'In which category does X belong?'. This aligns classification with the function of predication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer scope-focused terminology (Total/Partial) over ambiguous Universal/Particular in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Bain proposes the terms Total and Partial for propositions, reserving Universal and Particular for inductive use; what matters is whether the assertion is of the whole or part of what the subject denotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In logical analysis emphasize whether a predication applies to the whole extent (total/ universal in the sense of scope) or only part (partial/particular). This avoids confusion arising from the double meaning of 'universal'/'particular' between syllogistic and inductive contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: On definitions: consider both the connotation in common usage and additional scientific connotation (Bain's view and its critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bain: 'the definition in its full import, is the sum of all the properties connoted by the name; it exhausts the meaning of a word.' He treats additional discovered properties as part of a term's meaning. The author objects that meaning should be tied to common usage, not specialized scientific discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a definition is 'complete', distinguish (a) nominal/common connotation (what ordinary users understand) and (b) special/scientific connotation (properties discovered by inquiry). Beware of treating empirically discovered attributes as part of a term's ordinary meaning unless that special usage has become standard in the relevant discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real propositions from verbal propositions (information-bearing vs tautological)
rubrics_metrics.description: A real proposition conveys information about facts; a verbal proposition states what is already contained in the name's connotation and therefore adds no new information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate propositions by whether they add factual content beyond the term's common connotation. If the predicate is already implied by the subject's ordinary meaning, the proposition is verbal. Use this distinction to detect when an asserted inference is substantive or merely restating a name's connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common connotation determines ordinary meaning (not every uniformly accompanying fact is part of common meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: although 'ruminant' and 'cloven-hoofed' are always found together, 'ruminant' does not mean 'cloven-hoofed' in common usage; a newly discovered animal might be ruminant without cloven feet and still be called ruminant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ascribing meaning to general names for purposes of ordinary reasoning, rely on the properties commonly marked in the public mind rather than on contingent regularities uncovered by specialists. This prevents conflating empirical correlation with semantic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two competing views of 'real definition' — Whately vs De Morgan
rubrics_metrics.description: Whately: a Real Definition 'explains any thing more of the nature of the thing than is implied in the name' (goes beyond nominal meaning). De Morgan: a Real Definition may contain less than the nominal definition provided it suffices to distinguish the thing from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which standard of 'real definition' you adopt: either (a) expand beyond customary connotation to explain nature (Whately), or (b) provide a minimal distinguishing description sufficient for identification (De Morgan). Different purposes (philosophical explanation vs practical distinction) call for different standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: When syllogisms involve imaginary or modal subjects, qualify predicates to avoid illicit assertion of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: In syllogism about dragons, asserting 'A dragon is a serpent' must be qualified; predicating real properties of imaginary beings implicitly asserts their reality unless expressed as 'imagined to' or otherwise modalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust premises and conclusions to reflect modality (imagined, possible, nonexistent). When an attribute can be truly predicated only of a real object, qualify statements about imaginary subjects (e.g., 'are imagined to breathe flame'). This preserves logical validity and avoids covert category errors between definition and factual claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use equivalent propositional transformations (equipollency/obversion) correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: The different cases of Equipollency, or 'Equivalent Propositional Forms', are set forth; one common change of expression is obversion (from affirming a proposition to denying its negative, or v. v.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard valid transformations (obversion, conversion where appropriate, contraposition, etc.) to recognize equivalences and reformulate propositions without altering truth. Be cautious to apply only those transformations that are valid for the propositional form in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify oppositions among propositions correctly (contraries, subcontraries, contradictories, subalternate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists and relations: Contraries (All A is B / No A is B), Subtraries (Some A is B / Some A is not B), Contradictories, and subalternate relations are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing logical relations, use the standard taxonomy of oppositions to determine compatibility and implication relations among propositional forms (which pairs can be true or false together, which entail others, etc.). This aids in testing consistency and valid inference patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully treat singular propositions' relation to universal rules in syllogistic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Bain denies that Singular Propositions should be classed with Universal for ratiocination; the author notes that if a proper name (e.g., 'Socrates') connotes attributes, syllogisms using it may be merely verbal rather than genuine reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to treat singulars as functionally equivalent to universals in a given logical context. Examine whether the attributes ascribed are part of the proper name's connotation; if so, apparent syllogistic inference may add no informational content. Explicitly mark whether singular premises are being used extensionally or intensionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat claims of Existence with attention to their logical form (not always mere names or reducible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Bain regards existence-claims as often elliptical and reducible to co-existence or succession, but the author argues that Existence can be predicated apart from Causation or Co-existence and has distinct meaning (e.g., to exist is to be capable of exciting some sensation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or formulating existence-claims, consider whether they are shorthand for more complex claims (about co-existence, causation, historical presence) or whether they assert a distinct ontological claim. Phrase existence-questions in the most informative concrete form available (e.g., about propagation, causal agency, or observable relations) when that clarifies the issue.
